description: We are dancing with the SARs
summary: AquaTrace is a satellite-based environmental monitoring platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 – Dancing with the SARs. The project focuses on the Konya Closed Basin in Türkiye, where groundwater resources face increasing pressure from agricultural activities and changing climate conditions. By combining Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) observations, primarily from ESA Sentinel-1, with available groundwater, rainfall, and drought data, AquaTrace investigates possible relationships between water stress and land surface changes. The platform processes and compares satellite observations from different dates and, where suitable data is available, uses InSAR techniques to investigate ground deformation. Through interactive maps, time-series graphs, and regional comparisons, AquaTrace transforms complex satellite data into understandable environmental information. Its purpose is to help identify areas that may require further investigation, support environmental awareness, and contribute to more informed and sustainable water resource management.
details:
AquaTrace is an interactive geospatial monitoring platform designed to investigate groundwater stress, land surface deformation, and climate-related environmental changes across the Konya Closed Basin in Türkiye. The project addresses the growing challenges of groundwater depletion, intensive agricultural irrigation, and increasing environmental risks in one of the country's most important agricultural regions. By bringing satellite observations and climate information together in a clear and accessible interface, AquaTrace aims to transform complex Earth observation data into meaningful environmental insights.

The platform uses historical satellite radar observations and climate indicators to examine changes across the basin over time. It processes spatial and time-series datasets, including surface deformation measurements where suitable processed data is available, alongside meteorological variables such as precipitation and temperature. These indicators are presented through interactive maps, charts, and visual summaries in a web-based dashboard. This allows users to explore regional patterns, compare changes over time, and identify areas that may require further investigation. Satellite radar observations do not directly measure groundwater levels; instead, they can provide indirect evidence of surface changes that may be associated with groundwater-related processes when interpreted alongside other data.

AquaTrace was developed primarily using Python. Streamlit was used to build the interactive web application, while Pandas and NumPy supported data processing and numerical analysis. Plotly was used to create interactive charts and time-series visualizations. Visual Studio Code (VS Code) served as the development environment, and the application was designed with a lightweight structure suitable for deployment through Streamlit Community Cloud.

Artificial intelligence tools also supported the development process. Google Gemini was used as an AI-assisted tool for coding support, troubleshooting, and improving the presentation of technical information. Within the platform, geospatial processing, statistical analysis, and time-series modeling are used to interpret satellite and climate datasets. These analytical methods help connect complex Earth observation measurements with understandable indicators. AI-assisted development was applied in areas such as coding support, troubleshooting, and technical information organization, while the project's analytical foundation relies on geospatial data processing, statistical analysis, and time-series modeling. The project does not claim to use a trained machine-learning model unless such a model is specifically implemented and validated.

The project draws on several space-agency and scientific data resources. NASA POWER provides meteorological and climate-related time-series information, including temperature and precipitation variables. ESA Sentinel-1 radar observations provide historical SAR data for examining surface changes across the Konya Closed Basin, with the intended analysis period extending from 2014 to 2026 where suitable observations and processed products are available. The Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF) supports satellite data discovery and availability checks through scene and coverage information. ECMWF reanalysis data provides additional atmospheric and climate context. NASA-ISRO NISAR is considered as an important complementary L-band radar mission, particularly for future observation and integration opportunities; its data are included in the analysis only where suitable observations are actually available and processed.

The creative aspect of AquaTrace lies in its localized approach and its combination of different environmental data sources. Rather than presenting generic global water statistics, AquaTrace focuses specifically on the Konya Closed Basin and its agricultural and ecological challenges. It brings radar observations and climate indicators into one accessible interface, helping users explore how environmental conditions and surface changes vary across the region. Its interactive visualizations make technical information easier to understand for people who may not have a background in remote sensing or geospatial analysis.

Several factors shaped the development of the project, including the urgency of groundwater depletion, the importance of sustainable agricultural water use, the need to understand sinkhole-related environmental risks, and the accessibility of reliable scientific data. The team also considered data quality, spatial and temporal resolution, compatibility between different datasets, processing performance, and the need to communicate uncertainty clearly. The lightweight dashboard design was chosen to make the project practical to demonstrate and explore during the challenge.

AquaTrace offers several potential benefits. It makes satellite and climate information easier to explore, supports the comparison of environmental changes over time, and provides a cost-effective way to investigate regional patterns using openly accessible Earth observation resources. By bringing different datasets together, it can help researchers, regional planners, and other stakeholders identify areas that may deserve closer attention. It is intended to complement, rather than replace, field measurements and official groundwater monitoring systems.

The intended impact of AquaTrace is to support greater awareness of water stress and encourage more informed environmental planning in the Konya Closed Basin. By making complex satellite observations more understandable, the project aims to contribute to discussions about sustainable irrigation, agricultural planning, and long-term water resource management. In the future, it could be expanded with additional satellite missions, verified groundwater measurements, and improved deformation datasets to provide a more comprehensive picture of environmental change.

AquaTrace brings together several areas of science, innovation, and technology, including Earth observation, remote sensing, radar data analysis, geospatial computing, climate science, environmental monitoring, artificial intelligence-assisted development, and data visualization. By combining these disciplines in an accessible platform, the project demonstrates how space-based data and digital technologies can help communities better understand environmental challenges and explore possible paths toward a more sustainable future.
